title: Practice Set PMSJ2 — The Operations That Bring Data Home
description: Junior recognition track: the operations that bring distributed data to single-process memory. .collect() / .toPandas() crashes, broadcast() applied to the wrong side. Companion to PS5.

datasets.description: Schema reference (20 rows). Junior memory & skew scenarios reference NordGrid at junior production scale (500K meters across 4 regions, single cluster).
Substations reference (6 rows). Anchors broadcast-eligibility scenarios.

tasks.title: The .collect() That Crashed Production

description.context: Three operations in PySpark pull DISTRIBUTED data back to the SINGLE-process driver: `.collect()`, `.toPandas()`, and the iterator forms of `.take(n)` / `.head(n)` when `n` is large. Each ships every retrieved row across the network into the driver's JVM heap. On dev fixtures (a few thousand rows) the heap easily holds the result; in production (hundreds of thousands or millions of rows) the same code crashes the driver. The crash trace points to `DAGScheduler.collectAsync` and `ByteArrayOutputStream` because deserialization on the driver is where the heap finally fills. The diagnostic skill is reading any list-comprehension / loop / generator that wraps a `.collect()` and recognising it as a 'pull everything to the driver' operation.
description.task: Which line crashes the production driver, and what is the diagnostic signal that this line — not the others — is the cause?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
The pipeline runs daily with 500K rows. Dev fixture is 5K rows. Driver heap is the default 1GB. The crash trace points to ByteArrayOutputStream during deserialization on the driver.

Production Rows: 500,000

Dev Fixture Rows: 5,000

Driver Memory: 1g (default)

Crash Signature: java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space at ByteArrayOutputStream

evidence.label: snippet.py
evidence.content:
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from pyspark.sql.functions import col, sum, avg

spark = SparkSession.builder.appName('daily_summary').getOrCreate()

# Step 1: load and filter
meters = spark.read.parquet('silver/meters/2026-04-30/')
active = meters.filter(col('status') == 'ACTIVE')

# Step 2: enrich with substations
subs = spark.read.parquet('reference/substations/')
enriched = active.join(subs, on='substation_id', how='inner')

# Step 3: build the day's region list for the report header
regions = [row['region'] for row in enriched.select('region').distinct().collect()]
print(f'Regions today: {regions}')

# Step 4: aggregate per region
summary = enriched.groupBy('region').agg(
    sum('daily_kw').alias('total_kw'),
    avg('daily_kw').alias('avg_kw'))

# Step 5: write the summary
summary.write.mode('overwrite').parquet('gold/daily_summary/2026-04-30/')

# Step 6: log row count for audit
row_count = enriched.count()
print(f'Processed {row_count} meter readings')

fields.label: Which line crashes the production driver, and what is the diagnostic signal that this line — not the others — is the cause?
options: Line 22 (`.write.parquet()`) — Spark collects all summary rows to the driver before writing a single Parquet file; fix with `.repartition(1)` before `.write` so the driver does not hold every region's row.

Line 8 (`.filter()`) — Spark's filter builds an intermediate on the driver before pushing the predicate down; on 500K rows the intermediate overflows the default 1GB driver heap during predicate evaluation.

Line 26 (`.count()`) — every action re-executes the full plan from line 7; on prod this reads 500K rows twice and the driver OOMs holding both reads. Fix: `.cache()` the enriched DataFrame before line 22.

Line 15 — the list comprehension wraps `.collect()`, the canonical driver-side action; the trace's ByteArrayOutputStream + DAGScheduler.collectAsync names this exact chain. `.distinct()` reduces upstream, but collect remains the only operation that ships data to the driver.
fields.correctAnswer: Line 15 — the list comprehension wraps `.collect()`, the canonical driver-side action; the trace's ByteArrayOutputStream + DAGScheduler.collectAsync names this exact chain. `.distinct()` reduces upstream, but collect remains the only operation that ships data to the driver.
fields.rationale: Line 15 is the only line that pulls data to the driver.collect()`.
fields.distractorRationale: write as a driver-side operation.Parquet writes happen from executors directly to storage; the driver coordinates but does not hold the data.

tasks.psReference: PS5 (Transformations and Actions — what .collect() does), PSI8 lesson 9 (Driver Memory Traps).

tasks.title: broadcast() Was Applied to the Wrong Side

description.context: `broadcast(df)` takes ONE DataFrame as its argument and ships THAT DataFrame to every executor as the build side of a hash join. The argument MUST be the SMALL side. The mechanic: Catalyst materializes the wrapped DataFrame as a hashed relation on the driver, then broadcasts it across the cluster. If the engineer wraps the LARGE side, the driver tries to materialize a huge DataFrame on its own heap and OOMs before any executor work can start. The diagnostic at first glance is reading the broadcast() argument and confirming the wrapped DataFrame is the smaller of the two sides being joined.
description.task: Which snippet is correct, which crashes the driver, and what is the diagnostic signal that distinguishes them at first glance?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
broadcast() takes ONE DataFrame as its argument and ships THAT DataFrame to every executor. The argument should be the small side; if the engineer wraps the large side, the driver tries to materialize 500K rows as the build side and OOMs.

Meters Size: 500,000 rows (~80MB)

Substations Size: 200 rows (~12KB)

evidence.label: Snippet A
evidence.content:
from pyspark.sql.functions import broadcast

meters = spark.read.parquet('silver/meters/2026-04-30/')   # 500K rows
subs = spark.read.parquet('reference/substations/')         # 200 rows

result = meters.join(broadcast(subs), on='substation_id', how='inner')

result.write.parquet('gold/enriched/')

evidence.label: Snippet B
evidence.content:
from pyspark.sql.functions import broadcast

meters = spark.read.parquet('silver/meters/2026-04-30/')   # 500K rows
subs = spark.read.parquet('reference/substations/')         # 200 rows

result = broadcast(meters).join(subs, on='substation_id', how='inner')

result.write.parquet('gold/enriched/')

fields.label: Which snippet is correct, which crashes the driver, and what is the diagnostic signal that distinguishes them at first glance?
options: Both correct — `broadcast()` is a hint Catalyst evaluates against `autoBroadcastJoinThreshold`; if the wrapped DataFrame exceeds it, Catalyst silently downgrades to sort-merge. Neither crashes; runtime difference is at most ~5%.

Snippet A is correct — `broadcast(subs)` wraps the 200-row side, Catalyst materializes a 12KB hashed relation on the driver and ships it. Snippet B wraps the 500K-row meters and OOMs the driver during materialization.

Snippet B is correct — broadcasting meters ships the data to executors so each holds a local copy and the join runs in parallel with no shuffle. Snippet A wastes broadcast on the small side, leaving meters to shuffle.

Both crash — `broadcast()` forces collection to the driver regardless of which side is wrapped; the correct pattern is letting `autoBroadcastJoinThreshold` decide automatically rather than using the hint.
fields.correctAnswer: Snippet A is correct — `broadcast(subs)` wraps the 200-row side, Catalyst materializes a 12KB hashed relation on the driver and ships it. Snippet B wraps the 500K-row meters and OOMs the driver during materialization.
fields.rationale: The argument inside `broadcast()` must be the SMALL DataFrame.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Believes Catalyst silently downgrades broadcast hints.

tasks.psReference: PS5 (Transformations and Actions), PSI3 lesson 2 (Broadcast Joins — Deep Dive).
